Bitcoin - Witsand

By: Floris Kotze | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
From Witsand to Mossel Bay, we hit the road to find out why Bitcoin is catching on — and why some still say no.

Unique Selling Point:
It sounds crazy: a small South African town where you can buy groceries, fuel, even tip your waiter — all in Bitcoin. But it’s happening. We go see for ourselves.

Summary:
Small towns along South Africa’s Garden Route, led by Witsand, are quietly adopting Bitcoin for everyday use — from buying groceries to paying for boat repairs. While the rand remains the official currency, locals are turning to Bitcoin as a faster, bank-free way to transact. But not everyone’s convinced. Carte Blanche goes on the road to find out if this is the future of money, or just a digital detour.

Further information:
Further Info – Bitcoin Along the Garden Route:

Witsand (population ~500) now has one of the highest per-capita Bitcoin adoption rates in the world. Locals can pay for fuel, groceries, accommodation, gym sessions, and even tip service staff — all using Bitcoin via the Lightning Network.

The movement started in 2018 with a few early adopters. By 2021, shops began accepting Bitcoin, and by 2023-24, nearly 50 local businesses were on board.

Bitcoin Ekasi, near Mossel Bay, uses The Surfer Kids NPO to create a circular Bitcoin economy in a local township. Coaches are paid in Bitcoin and can spend it in the community, creating financial access in a place where many have never had bank accounts.

The idea is spreading — Plettenberg Bay now has over 70 businesses accepting Bitcoin. Stellenbosch and George are also growing hubs.

The system is supported by local WhatsApp groups, where community members educate each other and keep scammers out.

Critics argue Bitcoin is volatile, impractical, and risky. You'll be speaking to a local who isn’t convinced — to explore both sides of the story.

While Bitcoin isn't legal tender in SA, it’s being used as a payment tool — prices are still listed in rand, but the transaction happens in Bitcoin.

Script:


Opening
Plane landing - Lourensa walking out of airport holding up a coin
PTC (Lourensa): When I say Bitcoin, what comes to mind? Probably the value of Bitcoin, which today is R1.6 million per coin. And then perhaps like me, you also don't know how it works or how to spend it. And therein lies the clue as to why we've come to the garden route.
Cut to: YouTube clip Joe Nakamoto “This is Bitcoin land or Bitcoin Witsand as it's officially known on the southern coast of South Africa. The Bitcoin bee is everywhere. Even the ostriches like Bitcoin here. There's Bitcoin graffiti, a giant Bitcoin sign and the Bitcoin white paper is actually hanging on the wall in lots of restaurants and holiday homes.”
Lourensa PTC
About two hours from George lies the small town of Witsand renowned for its sea and landscapes. And the reason why we're on our way there. It's the only town in South Africa where the majority of businesses accept Bitcoin as currency.
So admittedly, I don't know much about Bitcoin. That's why I downloaded a few tips to bring me up to speed. We'll call it ‘Bitcoin for Dummies’.
Upsound:
‘What is Bitcoin? Bitcoin is often called digital gold because like gold, it has special qualities that make it valuable as money. It has a limited supply. There will never be more than 21 million Bitcoin.’


Lourensa PTC
So we finally arrived in Witsand and we're welcomed by a billboard where the Bitcoin logo is bigger than the word ‘Witsand’.
VO1:
To help us make sense of how this came to be, we're meeting someone who's played a big role in it.
Upsound:
Lourensa: Okay so now we are going to use Bitcoin.
Edwin: We are going to use Bitcoin!

VO2:
That's Edwin Jones, a software developer and self-confessed “Bitcoiner”. He's one of the first people who got local businesses to start accepting Bitcoin in Witsand.
Lourensa:
Edwin, how did Witsand become one of the towns about the town where Bitcoin is most commonly used?
Edwin
In 2018 there was a critical mass of people that actually understood Bitcoin well enough to start adopting it and become Bitcoin friendly. As a result, Bitcoiners from all over the world started coming to Witsand to have a Bitcoin friendly experience and to kind of have a window into the future.
VO 3:
And that future - means moving away from traditional money. Where the value isn’t set by banks — but by people USING Bitcoin.
Edwin
I think our money is a little bit broken at this moment. Like if people save in Rands, over time their Rands just get worth less. So people are incentivised to consume. If we can reverse that by having a money that is valuable itself, that could actually create a better world and leave consumables for people that need it more.
VO 4:
To get a glimpse of what that world might look like, we decided to try it for ourselves — We downloaded a wallet app - think of it as a digital purse. You scan and pay, and BITCOIN, minus the bank's charges, zips between users’ digital wallets — instantly. But you can't buy Bitcoin in the app. We had to use a separate crypto exchange app for that. We bought R5000 worth of Bitcoin and loaded it into our wallet. And what did that get us? 0.003 Bitcoin.
Yup. Not even close to one Bitcoin. But it’s what we’ve got — so let’s spend it! I guess that means lunch is on me.
Lourensa Upsound:
Thank you so much. Do you accept Bitcoin? Yes. Okay.
Lourensa Upsound:
All right, let me scan. Slide to confirm. Wow that was easy. Done? Okay.
VO 5:
It's not just Witsand where Bitcoin is starting to take hold. According to Edwin, other towns along the Garden Route are catching on too. So we hit the road to visit a few of them ourselves, and I'm still catching up on all this Bitcoin info as we go.
BTC for Dummies:
Why would anyone use Bitcoin? Bitcoin allows for fast and cheap transactions and taking back control of your money in a form that is designed to appreciate in value over time …
VO 6:
So Bitcoin offers you complete control of your own money - free transactions with no monthly fees in your own wallet App, almost like having your own bank.
Lourensa Upsound:
Oh wow. Look at that. Bitcoin everywhere.
Luthando
I'm the one that started receiving my salary in Bitcoin. Since 2022, it has moved all my salary in Bitcoin, 100%.
VO 7:
Luthando Ndabambi is a former surf coach, and is now Project Community Lead at a non-profit called The Surfer Kids. Since learning about Bitcoin, he's been helping business owners in his township adopt Bitcoin and teaching local kids how to use it too, through a project known as Bitcoin Ekasi.

Luthando:
Here at Bitcoin, we have 34 shops. They are accepting Bitcoin for payment. So we also like the staff that they are receiving their salary in Bitcoin. So people that are receiving Bitcoin, they have to spend those Bitcoin to the spaza shops.
Lourensa:
Why do you want people to adopt Bitcoin and to use Bitcoin?
Because it seems like Bitcoin is better money for everyone. And also anyone can get something from Bitcoin. If they can start using it, they can start saving on it. They will get something in the future.
VO 8:
According to Luthando, Bitcoin is better than money because it grows in value over time. Unlike traditional money, that loses value due to inflation. And with the wallet app, it's safer, especially for kids. No need to carry cash.
Drik Kotzé
In Mossel Bay it's very important that we get our economy growing. It's a bit of an innovative idea getting the youth and especially in the more poorer areas to get them involved.

Vo 9:
Dirk Kotzé is the executive mayor of Mossel Bay. He's seen Bitcoin Ekasi grow from an idea into a working system, and he's backing it all the way.
Drik Kotzé
Well, we try to be innovative. So I would like to challenge other mayors to see how you can use use innovation, use technology. It's accessible. You can use it any place. And also for your shop owners. They don't need very expensive equipment to help their clients and customers. And I think this is a fun and exciting way and interesting and techno innovation way to get them involved.

VO 10:
Anyone — of any age — can download a wallet app and start earning Bitcoin and spending it. The barrier to entry is way lower than with traditional banks.
Upsound Voxie Shop Owner
If I did not accept Bitcoin, this shop would have been closed by now. I would not have money in the bank.
VO 11:
We take a walk to see who's keen to get in on the Bitcoin action.
Upsound Lourensa
Hello. Do you accept Bitcoin? No. You don't accept Bitcoin?
No. He doesn't accept it. Okay. You think it's a scam?
Have you heard about Bitcoin?
I've heard about it.
What do you think it is?
Something like an account.


VO 12:
It’s early days for Bitcoin here. But it IS slowly growing.
I’m back on the road, learning more about Bitcoin as I go.


Bitcoin for dummies
“how does bitcoin work let's just say there's an app for that there are many different apps available today that enable us to use bitcoin….
Lourensa PTC:
Okay, so my understanding is slightly better, but I'm still quite confused.
VO13:
Back in Witsand, we set out to speak to some business owners to hear what they really think about adopting Bitcoin.
But we were shown the door.


Lourensa PTC
Ok, so not everyone in Witsand is as enthusiastic about Bitcoin.


VO 14:
A lot of people still steer clear of Bitcoin. Some think it’s a scam. Others worry it’s too volatile… or just too complicated to use. And then there’s the darker side — Just like cash, it’s been tied to crimes.
Voxie (Subtitle):
Witsand isn’t just, broadly speaking, a Bitcoin town. If it’s your money — the unit you choose to use that’s your choice. But don’t say Witsand is a Bitcoin town.

Edwin:
In small towns, you have small town politics and a lot of those opinions are more personality clashes and people just not willing to have the conversation.

Like when you start figuring out what Bitcoin is and what was wrong with the legacy system, you start questioning everything. And there are some cult-like behaviors in the…
Lourensa:
I wasn't going to use that word, but I'm glad you did.
Lourensa PTC:
So I still don't quite understand the technical ins and outs of Bitcoin, but it's clear that many people along the garden route feel very strongly about its potential, especially the community here in Witsand. And who knows, maybe one day we'll all be using Bitcoin, but I don't think that day is today.
Outro section
And there’s the money. You’ve got your money. We’ve got our breakfast. 100%. Everyone’s happy. Yeah, the money’s somewhere. It’s there, somewhere. Bitcoin. I still don’t really understand it, but... here we go. Thank you very much.








PROMO 1 – Living with Bitcoin
VO: Can Bitcoin really work in everyday life?

UPSOUND – Edwin Jones
“Once you're in the Bitcoin ecosystem, everything is extremely smooth... things just work.”
(Edwin Multicam.txt – 00:08:52:14 to 00:09:29:13)

VO: We visit Witsand along the Garden Route — to see how Bitcoin is being used, accepted, or simply ignored.

PROMO 2 – Township Wallets

VO: Can Bitcoin help people in places banks don’t reach?

UPSOUND – Mayor Dirk Kotzé
“We try to be innovative. So I would like to challenge other mayors... use technology. It’s accessible. You can use it any place.” (Mosselbaai Mayor.txt – 00:05:18)
VO: We visit Mossel Bay, along the Garden Route — to see how Bitcoin is starting to replace traditional banking in some communities.

PROMO 3 – Safer Than Cash
VO: Can Bitcoin be safer than cash?
UPSOUND – Luthando Ndabambi
“It’s not safe to walk around with cash. Especially for kids. With Bitcoin, they just need a phone.” (Luthando.txt – 01:05:50)
VO: We visit a few towns along the Garden Route to see how some are already living in the future.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): From Witsand to Mossel Bay, we hit the road to find out why Bitcoin is catching on — and why some still say no.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: It sounds crazy: a small South African town where you can buy groceries, fuel, even tip your waiter — all in Bitcoin. But it’s happening. We go see for ourselves.
metadata.Summary: Small towns along South Africa’s Garden Route, led by Witsand, are quietly adopting Bitcoin for everyday use — from buying groceries to paying for boat repairs. While the rand remains the official currency, locals are turning to Bitcoin as a faster, bank-free way to transact. But not everyone’s convinced. Carte Blanche goes on the road to find out if this is the future of money, or just a digital detour.
metadata.Further information: Further Info – Bitcoin Along the Garden Route: Witsand (population ~500) now has one of the highest per-capita Bitcoin adoption rates in the world. Locals can pay for fuel, groceries, accommodation, gym sessions, and even tip service staff — all using Bitcoin via the Lightning Network. The movement started in 2018 with a few early adopters. By 2021, shops began accepting Bitcoin, and by 2023-24, nearly 50 local businesses were on board. Bitcoin Ekasi, near Mossel Bay, uses The Surfer Kids NPO to create a circular Bitcoin economy in a local township. Coaches are paid in Bitcoin and can spend it in the community, creating financial access in a place where many have never had bank accounts. The idea is spreading — Plettenberg Bay now has over 70 businesses accepting Bitcoin. Stellenbosch and George are also growing hubs. The system is supported by local WhatsApp groups, where community members educate each other and keep scammers out. Critics argue Bitcoin is volatile, impractical, and risky. You'll be speaking to a local who isn’t convinced — to explore both sides of the story. While Bitcoin isn't legal tender in SA, it’s being used as a payment tool — prices are still listed in rand, but the transaction happens in Bitcoin.
